summary: Describes how a LoST client can discover a LoST server using DHCP. Placing a server close to the user in the access network can help emergency communication stay working when connectivity is poor. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Your phone needs to know which helper to ask about emergency numbers. This lets the network hand over the helper's address when you connect.

questions: how does a lost client find a lost server
how is a domain name encoded in a dhcp option
subtitle: How a DHCP server hands a device the domain name of a nearby emergency-location lookup server.

tldr.problem: A LoST client needs to find a LoST server, which maps a service and a location to contact URLs, and a server close to the user in the access network is desirable, especially in disasters with intermittent connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a DHCPv4 option (code 137) and a DHCPv6 option (code 51) that carry one domain name, encoded as in RFC 1035. The client feeds that name into the DNS-based LoST discovery procedure.
tldr.outcome: The access network can point clients at its own LoST server, or one it knows about. The RFC's security section warns that a forged DHCP response could lead a client to a rogue server.

today: RFC 5223 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Discover a LoST Server with DHCP
sections.content:
The Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol, defined in RFC 5222, is an XML-based protocol that maps a service identifier and a geospatial or civic location to service contact URLs. To use it, a LoST client first has to learn the address of a LoST server. The RFC notes that several mechanisms can do this, including manual configuration.

Where the access network runs a LoST server, or knows a third party that does, DHCP can give the end host a domain name. That name is then the input to the DNS-based resolution mechanism in RFC 5222, which reuses the URI-enabled NAPTR specification from RFC 4848. This RFC specifies a DHCPv4 option and a DHCPv6 option with the same functionality.
sections.eli5: Before you can ask the emergency helper a question, you have to know where to find it. The network you just joined can tell you.

sections.title: Domain Name Encoding
sections.content:
Both options carry the domain name in the encoding of Section 3.1 of RFC 1035. Each label is a one-octet length followed by that many octets. Because every domain name ends with the null label of the root, the name ends with a length byte of zero.

The high-order two bits of every length octet MUST be zero, which leaves six bits and limits a label to 63 octets or less. To simplify implementations, the whole name (label octets plus length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less.
sections.eli5: A name is written as chunks, and each chunk starts with a number saying how long it is. A zero means the name is finished.

sections.title: The DHCPv4 Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 option carries a fully-qualified domain name for the client to use to locate a LoST server. It has three parts: the code, OPTION_V4_LOST with value 137; a length, which counts the octets of the whole domain name field; and the LoST Server Domain Name itself, made of the labels s1, s2, s3 and so on.

The length field in the option covers the entire encoded name, while the length bytes inside the encoding each cover one label. A DHCPv4 client MAY ask for the option in a Parameter Request List option, as described in RFC 2131. The option holds a single domain name and so MUST contain precisely one root label.
sections.eli5: The note the network sends has a label saying what it is, a number saying how long the name is, and then the name.

sections.title: The DHCPv6 Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option does the same job. Its option-code is OPTION_V6_LOST, value 51. The option-length field gives the length of the domain name field in octets, and the LoST Server Domain Name follows, encoded as in Section 3 of the RFC.

A DHCPv6 client MAY request the name in an Options Request Option (ORO), as described in RFC 3315. As with DHCPv4, the option contains a single domain name and MUST contain precisely one root label.
sections.eli5: The newer kind of network uses a different envelope with a different label number, but the message inside is the same name.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content: The RFC shows a DHCPv4 option where the server offers the name example.com as input to the U-NAPTR LoST discovery procedure. The bytes are the code 137, a length of 13, then the labels: 7 followed by example, 3 followed by com, and a closing 0.
sections.eli5: To send the name example.com, the network sends the length of each word before the word, then a zero to say it is done.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned both option codes. For DHCPv4 the option is OPTION_V4_LOST with value 137, described in Section 4. For DHCPv6 it is OPTION_V6_LOST with value 51, described in Section 5.
sections.eli5: A central office keeps the official list of label numbers, and these two numbers were reserved for this job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an adversary modifies a response from a DHCP server, or inserts its own response, a LoST client could be led to contact a rogue LoST server under the adversary's control, or be given an invalid address. These threats are documented in RFC 5069.

The security considerations in RFC 2131, RFC 2132 and RFC 3315 also apply, and RFC 5222 enumerates the LoST security mechanisms.
sections.eli5: If a trickster pretends to be the network, they could send you to the wrong helper, so be careful who you trust to hand you the card.
